Most music asks you to listen. **Ambient music** lets you choose. Brian Eno, who gave it its name,
wrote in the notes to *Music for Airports* that it "must be able to accommodate many levels of
listening attention without enforcing one in particular; it must be as ignorable as it is
interesting." That one sentence explains most of the production tricks on this page: no strong beat
to grab you, no melody that demands to be followed, and a sound that keeps changing so slowly that
it never quite repeats.

**How to use the page.** Read the history first, then try each technique in its own widget. The
last section puts them all together in the **Ambient Generator**; it also has its own page,
[Ambient Generator](../tools/ambient.qmd).

## A short history

**Furniture music (1917).** Erik Satie coined *musique d'ameublement*, "furniture music", in 1917:
music meant to sit in the background of a room like the furniture. A set was played in Paris in 1920
as intermission music.

**Drones and tape (the 1960s).** La Monte Young built music from sustained tones held for a very long
time; Eno later called him "the daddy of us all". In 1962 the San Francisco Tape Music Center brought
together composers who worked with tape recorders, among them Pauline Oliveros, Terry Riley and Steve
Reich. Repeating patterns, drones and calm consonant harmony from this minimal music all fed into
ambient. Oliveros later (1988) coined **deep listening** after recording in an underground cistern
with a reverb some 45 seconds long.

**Berlin (the 1970s).** German electronic musicians, Tangerine Dream and Klaus Schulze among them (the
"Berlin School"), made long pieces from looping sequencer patterns and synthesizer washes.

**Eno names it (1975–1979).** In January 1975 Eno was in bed after a car accident. A friend put on a
record of eighteenth-century harp music; it was far too quiet, it was raining outside, and he could
not get up to turn it up. He heard the music as part of the room. (The friend, Judy Nylon, remembers
it differently.) The same year he made *Discreet Music*: a synthesizer playing two short phrases of
**different lengths**, through an EQ and an echo, recorded on one tape machine and played back on a
second machine whose output fed back into the first, so every phrase came round again, softer, on
top of the new ones. *Ambient 1: Music for Airports* (released February 1979) was the first album
he put out under the label "ambient". It was made from **tape loops of different lengths**: in
"2/1" each loop held a sung note, and Eno started them all running and, in his words, "let them
configure in the way they chose to configure". Because the loop lengths do not divide into each
other, the notes keep landing in new combinations.

**The chill-out room (around 1990).** In British dance culture, the quiet room away from the main
floor, the **chill-out room**, played ambient, dub and slow beats. By the early 1990s the Orb, Aphex
Twin and others were being called *ambient house* or *ambient techno*; Aphex Twin's *Selected Ambient
Works Volume II* came out in 1994.

## The techniques

| Technique | What it does | Where you've met it on this site |
|---|---|---|
| **Drone** | one or two held notes (root and fifth) underneath everything, so there is never a chord change to wait for | [Ragas](ragas.qmd) (the tanpura) |
| **Loops of unequal length** | short phrases that repeat, each at its own length, so they line up differently every time round | this page |
| **Slow change** | filters and levels that move over tens of seconds, too slowly to hear as a movement | [LFOs](sound-lfo.qmd) |
| **Long reverb** | puts every note in a huge space; notes overlap into a wash | [Reverb](sound-reverb.qmd) |
| **Tape echo** | each note comes back softer and darker, a little out of tune | [Delay](sound-delay.qmd) |
| **Shaped noise** | rain, wind, surf or tape hiss as a bed under the notes | [Noise](sound-noise.qmd), below |
| **Soft attacks, safe scales** | no sharp starts; pentatonic or Lydian notes that never clash, whatever lands together | [Envelopes](sound-envelopes.qmd) |

## Noise you can shape

Noise has energy at every frequency, so an **equaliser** can carve almost any texture out of it. This
one has ten bands, an octave apart from 31 Hz to 16 kHz, like a graphic EQ on a mixing desk. Push a
band up (+) to bring that part of the noise forward, pull it down (−) to take it away. The pink line
on the spectrum is the curve you've drawn.

<div class="sk" data-w="noiseeq"></div>

- **Rain on a roof**: cut the lows, lift 2–8 kHz. **Distant surf**: the opposite, plus a slow swell.
- **Wind** is a hump in the middle (250 Hz–1 kHz) that rises and falls.
- **Tape hiss** is just the top: a sound ambient producers sometimes *add* back, for warmth.

This noise never repeats. (Earlier versions of the site's noise were a few seconds of noise played on
a loop; the ear catches the repeat as a soft "whoosh" every two or three seconds. See
[Noise](sound-noise.qmd).)

## Loops of unequal length

Try the generator below with only the loops: turn **Drone** and **Noise bed** to 0. Each ring is one
loop; a dot is a note; the bright mark is the playhead going round. Now drag **Loop lengths** to *all
equal*: every loop comes round together and you hear a steady pulse, like a song. Drag it back to *far
apart*: the notes keep finding new neighbours, and the music never quite repeats. That is the
*Music for Airports* method.

## The Ambient Generator

<div class="sk" data-w="ambient" data-preset="Airport (tape loops)"></div>

- **Key** and **Scale**: the notes the loops choose from. Pentatonic and Lydian have no notes that
  clash badly, so any notes that happen to land together sound fine.
- **Tape loops**, **Loop lengths**, **Notes per loop**: how many loops, how different their lengths
  are (from 19 seconds to about 45), and how busy each one is.
- **Drone**: root, fifth and octave on detuned sawtooth waves, each behind a low-pass filter that opens
  and closes over half a minute or more.
- **Noise bed**: open *Noise bed* for its colour, swell and the same 10-band EQ as above.
- **Reverb** and **Reverb length**, **Tape echo**: the space. The echo feeds the reverb, as it would
  on a studio desk.

## Try this

1. Start *Airport*. Wait a full minute without touching anything. Do you hear the same moment twice?
2. Turn **Reverb** to 0. What happens to the mood? Bring it back slowly.
3. Choose *Rain room*, open the noise bed and move the **8k** band. When does the rain stop sounding
   like rain and start sounding like hiss?
4. Make your own: choose a key, scale and instrument, set the loops, and describe what you made in
   one sentence that Eno might have written.
